tips.title: Tops with tops, bottoms with bottoms
tips.body: Adding and subtracting column vectors never mixes the two rows. $\binom{3}{1} + \binom{1}{4} = \binom{4}{5}$. A scalar multiplies **both** rows. Nothing ever crosses over.

tips.title: The middle letter cancels
tips.body: $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$: go A to B to C and you have gone A to C. And reversing negates, so $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$. Nearly every diagram question is built from those two facts.

tips.title: AB is b minus a
tips.body: With $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$, the vector $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ — undo a, then do b. The midpoint of AB is then $\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b})$, the average. Both are worth knowing by heart.

tips.title: Say the word parallel
tips.body: Showing $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\overrightarrow{RS}$ earns the working mark; **therefore PQ is parallel to RS** earns the conclusion mark. Examiners report the missing sentence as the commonest loss in vector questions. Factorise first, so the multiple is visible.

steps.title: What a vector is
steps.body:
A **vector** has both a **size** and a **direction**. A number alone — a **scalar** — has only size.

Written as a **column vector**, the top number is the movement **across** and the bottom number the movement **up**:

$$\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

means 3 to the right and 1 up. Negative numbers mean left and down.

Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same size **and** the same direction. That means a vector can be drawn anywhere on the page: it is the movement that matters, not where it starts. Two arrows of the same length pointing the same way represent the **same vector**, even if they are drawn in different places.

Notation you need to read:

- **bold a**, or $\underline{a}$ when written by hand
- $\overrightarrow{AB}$ — the vector **from A to B**

The arrow direction matters: $\overrightarrow{BA}$ is the same length but points the opposite way, so $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$.

steps.title: Adding and subtracting
steps.body:
Adding column vectors is done **separately, top and bottom**. Nothing crosses over.

$$\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$$

Subtracting works the same way, and it helps to think of it as **adding the negative**:

$$\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} + (-\mathbf{b}) = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$$

steps.title: Multiplying by a scalar
steps.body:
Multiplying a vector by a **scalar** — an ordinary number — multiplies **both** parts:

$$2\mathbf{a} = 2\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$$

What that does geometrically is the important part.

- The vector becomes **$k$ times as long**.
- Its **direction is unchanged** if $k$ is positive.
- Its direction is **reversed** if $k$ is negative.

So $2\mathbf{a}$ is twice as long and points the same way; $-\mathbf{a}$ is the same length and points the opposite way.

**Any scalar multiple of a vector is parallel to it.** That single fact does most of the work in vector geometry, because showing two vectors are multiples of each other proves the lines are parallel.

The **magnitude** — the length — is found with Pythagoras:

$$\left| \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} \right| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$$

and doubling the vector doubles the magnitude.

steps.title: Vectors on a diagram
steps.body:
On a diagram, $\overrightarrow{AB}$ means the journey **from A to B**. Journeys join up:

$$\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$$

Go from A to B, then from B to C, and you have gone from A to C. The **B in the middle cancels**, which is the single most useful pattern in the whole topic.

Two consequences worth having ready.

- **Reversing** a journey negates the vector: $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$.
- To get from B to C **via A**, go backwards then forwards: $\overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{BA} + \overrightarrow{AC} = -\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AC}$.

That second one is how most diagram questions are solved: you are given two vectors from a common point and asked for the one joining their ends.

A journey that returns to where it started is the **zero vector**: going all the way round a triangle gives $\mathbf{0}$.

steps.title: Midpoints and fractions of a line
steps.body:
Questions often mark a point part of the way along a line. The method is always the same: get to the start of the line, then go a fraction of the way along it.

If M is the **midpoint** of AB, then

$$\overrightarrow{AM} = \tfrac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}$$

and to reach M from O you go to A first, then half of AB.

steps.title: Going deeper: parallel, and proving it
steps.body:
**Parallel means scalar multiple.** Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a number times the other. $6\mathbf{a}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{a}$; so is $-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}$, pointing the other way.

That is the whole of what a vector proof needs. To show two lines are parallel, get a vector for each and show one is a multiple of the other.

> If $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\mathbf{a} + 4\mathbf{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{RS} = \mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b}$, then $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\overrightarrow{RS}$, so **PQ is parallel to RS**, and twice as long.

**The sentence matters.** Writing $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\overrightarrow{RS}$ and stopping earns the working mark but not the conclusion. You must say *therefore PQ is parallel to RS*. Examiners report this as the commonest lost mark in vector questions.

**Collinear points.** If $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ are multiples of each other, then A, B and C lie on a **straight line** — because the two parts of the journey point the same way and they share the point B. The word for that is **collinear**, and questions ask you to prove it.

**A caution.** $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$ is **not** parallel to $\mathbf{a}$, and it is not longer than $|\mathbf{a}| + |\mathbf{b}|$ either unless the two point the same way. Vectors do not add like lengths: $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has magnitude $\sqrt{10}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\sqrt{17}$, but their sum $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ has magnitude $\sqrt{41}$, which is less than $\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{17}$.

**Simplify before concluding.** A vector answer like $\tfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{b}$ hides the factor. Written as $\tfrac{2}{3}(\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b})$ the multiple is visible, and the parallel conclusion becomes obvious.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **vector** has size and direction; a **scalar** has size only.
- In a **column vector**, the top number is across and the bottom is up.
- Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same size and direction, wherever they are drawn.
- **Add and subtract** separately, tops with tops and bottoms with bottoms.
- Subtracting is **adding the negative**.
- A **scalar multiple** makes a vector $k$ times as long, **reversing** it if $k$ is negative.
- **Any scalar multiple is parallel** to the original.
- **Magnitude**: $|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, by Pythagoras.
- $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$: the **middle letter cancels**.
- $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$.
- With $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$, and the **midpoint** of AB is $\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b})$.
- To prove lines **parallel**, show one vector is a multiple of the other — then **write the conclusion**.
- **Factorise** a vector answer so the common factor is visible.
- Vectors do **not** add like lengths: $|\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}|$ is usually less than $|\mathbf{a}| + |\mathbf{b}|$.

questions.prompt: On a diagram, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$. N is the point one third of the way from A to B. Find $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, simplifying your answer.
questions.solution: To reach N from O, first travel from O to A, which is the vector a, and then travel one third of the way along AB. The vector from A to B is found by going backwards along OA and then forwards along OB, which gives minus a plus b, or b minus a. One third of that is one third of b minus a. So the vector ON is a plus one third of b minus a. Expanding the bracket gives a plus one third b minus one third a. Collecting the a terms gives two thirds a plus one third b. This can be written more neatly as one third of the quantity two a plus b, which shows the structure of the answer clearly.

criteria.text: Writes ON as OA plus a fraction of AB

questions.modelAnswer:
**The journey.** O to A, then one third of the way from A to B:

$$\overrightarrow{ON} = \mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\overrightarrow{AB}$$

**Finding AB.** Undo a, then do b:

$$\overrightarrow{AB} = -\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$$

**Substituting and simplifying.**

$$\overrightarrow{ON} = \mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{b} - \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{a} = \tfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{b}$$

$$= \tfrac{1}{3}(2\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b})$$

Factorising at the end is worth doing: it makes any scalar multiple visible, which is what a later parallel or collinear part would need.

questions.prompt: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 4\mathbf{a} + 6\mathbf{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{RS} = 2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}$. Show that PQ is parallel to RS, and state how their lengths compare.
questions.solution: Look for a common factor in the vector PQ. Four a plus six b can be written as two times the quantity two a plus three b, because two is a factor of both four and six. The expression inside the bracket, two a plus three b, is exactly the vector RS. Therefore the vector PQ is equal to two times the vector RS. Since one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, the two lines PQ and RS are parallel. Because the scalar is two, the line PQ is also twice as long as the line RS. It is important to state the conclusion about being parallel explicitly, since showing the multiple alone does not answer the question that was asked.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Factorise.** Two divides both 4 and 6:

$$\overrightarrow{PQ} = 4\mathbf{a} + 6\mathbf{b} = 2(2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b})$$

**Recognise the bracket.** $2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}$ is exactly $\overrightarrow{RS}$, so

$$\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\overrightarrow{RS}$$

**Conclude — and this is a separate mark.** One vector is a **scalar multiple** of the other, **therefore PQ is parallel to RS**.

**Lengths.** The scalar is 2, so **PQ is twice as long as RS**.

Showing the multiple without writing the parallel conclusion is the commonest lost mark in vector questions.

examTechnique.body:
For column vectors, work the two rows separately and keep the signs visible.

On a diagram, build every answer out of journeys you have been given, choosing a route where the middle letters cancel.

Write $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ down as soon as you see O, A and B. Most parts build on it.

For a point part of the way along a line, get to the start of the line first, then take the fraction of the whole vector.

**Factorise your answer.** A common factor is what a parallel or collinear argument needs, and it is invisible until you take it out.

And when you have shown a scalar multiple, write the sentence: *therefore the lines are parallel*. The working alone does not answer the question.
examinerErrors: Mixing the rows when adding column vectors.
Forgetting that reversing a journey negates the vector.
Taking a fraction of the wrong vector for a point along a line.
Leaving an answer unfactorised, so the scalar multiple stays hidden.
Showing the multiple but never writing the word parallel.
Using a scalar where a vector belongs, or the reverse.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ before it is asked for, because almost every later part depends on it, and it builds each new vector as a journey rather than guessing at a combination. It factorises the final expression as a matter of habit, which turns a messy answer into visible evidence of a scalar multiple. And it finishes a proof with the conclusion in words — parallel, or collinear with a shared point — knowing that the algebra is the working and the sentence is the answer.
